names: severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV)
profile.headline: Tick-borne bandavirus causing a severe haemorrhagic febrile illness in East Asia, with case fatality of roughly 5–30%.
profile.syndrome: Fever, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, gastrointestinal symptoms and elevated liver enzymes, progressing in severe cases to haemorrhage, encephalopathy and multi-organ failure. Older age and high viral load predict death.
profile.transmission: Haemaphysalis longicornis tick bite; person-to-person transmission through blood and body fluids is documented, including nosocomial and familial clusters, and transmission from infected cats and dogs to humans.
profile.reservoir: Domestic and wild animals (goats, cattle, dogs, cats, deer, rodents).
profile.geography: China, South Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Taiwan.
profile.management: Supportive. Favipiravir has been trialled with uncertain benefit; plasma exchange used in severe cases.
profile.prevention: Tick avoidance, protective measures in animal handling, strict infection control for contact with patients' blood and secretions.
evidence: Identified in 2009–2011 from clusters in central China; thousands of confirmed cases with documented person-to-person and animal-to-human transmission.

root/riboviria/orthornavirae/negarnaviri.name: Bandavirus heartlandense

profile.headline: North American counterpart of SFTSV, transmitted by the lone star tick.
profile.syndrome: Fever, fatigue, anorexia, thrombocytopenia and leukopenia; deaths reported, mostly in older adults with comorbidity.
profile.reservoir: White-tailed deer, raccoons and other wildlife (serological evidence).
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR and serology at CDC/state laboratories.
profile.management: Supportive; doxycycline is ineffective, which matters because the illness mimics ehrlichiosis.
evidence: First two cases reported in Missouri in 2012 with virus isolation; dozens of confirmed cases since.

profile.headline: A leading cause of summer aseptic meningitis around the Mediterranean, transmitted by sandflies.
profile.syndrome: Aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis, usually self-limiting; also undifferentiated 'summer fever'.
profile.reservoir: Sandflies maintain the virus; vertebrate reservoirs incompletely defined (dogs and cats implicated).
profile.geography: Italy, Spain, France, Portugal, Greece, Turkey, North Africa.
profile.prevention: Sandfly avoidance (fine mesh is needed — standard nets let sandflies through), repellents.
evidence: Routinely identified in CSF of Mediterranean meningitis patients; in some series the second most common cause after enteroviruses.

highlights.name: Phlebovirus riftense
highlights.headline: Zoonotic phlebovirus causing devastating ruminant abortion storms and human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen.

root/riboviria/orthornavirae/negarnaviri.name: Phlebovirus riftense

profile.headline: Zoonotic phlebovirus causing devastating ruminant abortion storms and human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen.
profile.syndrome: Most human infections are a self-limiting febrile illness. Complications: retinitis with permanent visual loss (1–10%), meningoencephalitis, and haemorrhagic fever with hepatic failure (<1%, but ~50% fatal).
profile.transmission: Mosquito bite (Aedes, Culex) but most human infections follow direct contact with blood, tissues or aborted material from infected livestock — slaughtering, butchering, veterinary and husbandry work; also raw milk.
vectors: Aedes mcintoshi (and other floodwater Aedes, with transovarial maintenance)
profile.reservoir: Sheep, goats, cattle, camels; virus persists in Aedes eggs between rains.
profile.geography: Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar, Egypt, Arabian peninsula; outbreaks follow heavy rainfall and flooding.
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR and IgM ELISA; antigen detection.
profile.management: Supportive; occupational exposure requires biosafety precautions.
profile.prevention: Livestock vaccination, movement controls, protective equipment during slaughter, vector control. No licensed human vaccine.
evidence: Large laboratory-confirmed human outbreaks (Egypt 1977, Kenya/Somalia 1997–98 and 2006–07) with defined occupational risk factors.

refs.label: WHO Rift Valley fever fact sheet

geo.text: Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar, Egypt, Arabian peninsula; outbreaks follow heavy rainfall and flooding.
